newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wheat sowings plunge, grain stockpiles shrink.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat sowings plunge, grain stockpiles shrink.

text.p: American farmers sowed only 48.2 million acres of winter wheat -- a stunning 7 percent decline that hinted at tight supplies -- the Agriculture Department said Friday, adding that the corn and soybean stockpiles would quickly dwindle to scanty levels.

Futures prices soared on the Chicago Board of Trade following release of the reports. Corn and soybeans immediately hit the daily limit for price increases while wheat was up as much as 15-1/2 cents per bushel.
"The biggest shocker ... was the winter wheat acreage number, the lowest since 1978," said Dan Basse of the Chicago-based analytical firm AgResource Co.

Grain and soybean prices have gyrated for the past two years because of tight U.S. supplies, but food prices have been fairly stable. Even though U.S. farmers grew the third-largest corn crop on record and the second-largest soybean crop in 1996, supplies are expected to stay barely ahead of voracious demand.

The winter wheat figure provided the first look at possible crop output for the new year. Analysts had expected 51.4 million acres would be planted to winter wheat, about the same as the 52 million planted for last year's crop.
Private analyst John Schnittker said the lower acreage could reduce U.S. wheat output by 120 million bushels.

Winter wheat, which is planted in the fall and harvested the following summer, is the major U.S. wheat crop. Small acreage could lead to a small harvest unless yields climb or spring wheat acreage expanded.

One Agriculture Department official said spring wheat acreage often rebounded when winter wheat acreage slumped, but another was less willing to speculate because the so-called "Freedom to Farm" agricultural policy reform law gave farmers more chances to plant non-wheat crops.
The law put the first cap ever on annual farm subsidy spending in exchange for removing most federal control over agriculture.

The Agriculture Department forecast U.S. stockpiles would shrink to 374 million bushels of wheat, 155 million bushels of soybeans and 959 million bushels of corn before the new crops mature. The corn and soybean estimates were 1 percent to 2 percent smaller than one month ago.

Mike Hoover, an analyst with the WEFA Group in suburban Philadelphia, said smaller stockpiles would support prices. WEFA anticipates farmers will plant about 80 million acres of corn and 64 million acres of soybeans.
"We expect to see a significant amount of corn planted as well as soybeans," Hoover said. "That should add some downward pressure on prices this fall."

About 1.82 billion bushels of soybeans and 6.91 billion bushels of corn were in the nation's bins and warehouses on Dec. 1. The "stocks" figures were slightly smaller than analysts expected, which helped propel prices higher on futures markets.

In its final look at 1996 crop output, the department raised its corn estimate slightly to 9.29 billion bushels, marginally reduced soybeans to 2.382 billion bushels and held wheat at 2.281 billion bushels.
